‘I must leave without knowing my fate, but I will return here, or follow your party, as soon as I can. A word or a glance will decide whether I enter your father’s house tonight or never again.’

She could not quickly recover from a letter like this. Half an hour alone to reflect might have calmed her, but the ten minutes before she was interrupted, under all the constraints of her situation, brought no peace. Instead, every moment stirred fresh emotion. Her happiness was overwhelming. Before that first flood of feeling had subsided, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all came in.

The absolute need to appear her usual self immediately forced her to struggle for composure, but before long she could sustain the effort no further. She stopped understanding anything they said, and had to excuse herself by saying she felt unwell. They could now see that she looked very ill. Alarmed and concerned, they would not have dreamed of leaving without her. This was dreadful. If only they had gone away and left her alone in that quiet room, she would have recovered. Having them all stand or wait around her was unbearable, and in desperation she announced that she would go home.

‘Certainly, my dear,’ Mrs. Musgrove cried. ‘Go home at once and look after yourself, so that you will be well enough for tonight. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I am no doctor. Charles, ring the bell and order a sedan chair. She must not walk.’

A chair, however, was out of the question. Nothing could be worse! She could not bear to lose the chance of exchanging a few words with Captain Wentworth as she walked quietly and alone up through the town, where she felt almost certain she would meet him. She protested earnestly against the chair. Mrs. Musgrove, who could think of only one kind of illness, anxiously made sure that no fall had occurred—that Anne had not recently slipped and struck her head, and was quite certain she had suffered no fall at all. Reassured, she could let Anne go cheerfully and expect to see her better that evening.

Determined not to overlook any possible precaution, Anne made an effort and said—

‘I am afraid, ma’am, that there may be some misunderstanding. Please tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your entire party this evening. I fear there has been a mistake, and I particularly wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope they will both come.’

‘Oh, my dear, everyone understands perfectly, I promise you.’

I have mentioned that he was a poet. He published his first poem at twenty-three, and the whole country greeted it with delighted enthusiasm. Good fortune never seemed to leave him. No one had ever become famous so quickly, or won such universal praise. Ordinary readers admired the very poems that astonished the scholar studying alone in his room. Not a single voice disagreed.

At this moment, when his fame was at its height, he met Elinor. She was an exceptionally beautiful young heiress who lived in the care of her guardian. From their first appearance together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not share Woodville’s genius, but she had a generous and noble character. Her youth and the love she inspired everywhere had kept her familiar only with goodness and excellence. She was lovely, with open, natural manners. Her deep blue eyes shone with a light that could come only from the union of deep feeling and wisdom.

They were suited to each other, and love soon followed. For the first time Woodville experienced its delight. Elinor was overjoyed to hold the heart of someone so handsome and so admired among his fellow men. What could such a union bring except perfect happiness?

Woodville was a poet whom every social circle wanted to welcome; whenever he appeared, every eye turned toward him. Yet he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a wealthy heiress. Her guardian did not object to their love. Woodville’s gifts were too remarkable for his smaller fortune to be counted against him. But her father’s will forbade her to marry before she came of age, and she would receive her fortune only if she obeyed. She had just begun her twentieth year, so the lovers had to accept the delay. Still, they were always together, and their happiness seemed like Paradise. They studied side by side and planned how they would spend their future. Taking in love and joy from each other’s eyes and words, they scarcely complained that their complete union must wait. Woodville’s fame continued to rise, while the lessons of her gifted lover made Elinor more lovely and more wise.

In two months Elinor would turn twenty-one. Everything stood ready for their marriage. How can I describe the disaster that ended so much joy? Yet this earth, covered in sorrow and ruin, would not be the earth we know if two such angelic beings had been allowed to live for each other. Search the whole world: you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have given them. To permit such complete joy would have required a revolution in the order of life established for us miserable inhabitants of the earth.

Yet he kept one secret from these dear friends, a secret he had cherished since his earliest years. Although he loved his fellow students, he trusted none of them to receive it with sufficient sensitivity or sympathy. He was in love. He feared they might ridicule the intensity of his feelings, and could not bear the thought of their desecrating what gave his life its meaning by treating it as something shallow and temporary.

Near his family home lived a gentleman of modest means who had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty merely complemented her other qualities: her intelligence was clear and strong, her temperament angelically gentle. She and my father had played together from infancy. Even as a child, Diana had been a favourite of his mother, whose affection for the beautiful, lively girl grew as she grew older. Consequently, throughout his school and college holidays they were constantly together. Novels, and all the other ways in which young people in civilized society learn about passions before experiencing them, had deeply affected him, particularly susceptible as he was to every impression. At eleven, Diana was his favourite playmate, but already he spoke the language of love. Though nearly two years older, her upbringing had left her more childlike, at least in understanding and expressing emotion. She innocently received his passionate declarations and returned them without knowing their meaning. Having read no novels and mixed only with her younger sisters, how could she distinguish love from friendship? By the time her developing understanding revealed the true nature of their relationship, her heart already belonged to her friend. Her only fear was that new attractions or a changeable heart might lead him to break the promises of his childhood.

Instead, those promises grew more passionate and tender every day. His love had matured alongside him, intertwining with every ability and every feeling until only death could remove it. No one knew of their love except the two of them. In this, as in everything else, he feared his companions’ disapproval: they might condemn his devotion to someone poorer than himself. Nevertheless, nothing could weaken, even for a moment, his intention of marrying her as soon as he gathered enough courage to face the difficulties he was determined to overcome.

Diana fully deserved the deepest love he could give her.
